children: The horizon over which the Federal Open Market Committee expects to achieve mandate-consistent levels of inflation and employment could be a useful additional element, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President Alberto Musalem.

"I consider an 18-month horizon reasonable. This is long enough to avoid constant readjustments of the policy stance, and short enough that we can be held to it," said Musalem, adding that specifying a horizon also helps maintain a forward-looking monetary policy posture.
Musalem was speaking before the London School of Economics and Political Science.
The speech comes amid a lively debate in the U.S. about how and what the Fed should communicate about its monetary policy. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh
defended his view that the so-called "forward guidance", or signaling the likely direction of the FOMC's policy path, isn't useful.

"A central bank should communicate how it turns incoming information into policy," said Musalem, adding that he is not referring to forward guidance but the framework for how and why policy is determined.
"A clearly communicated framework yields smoother monetary policy transmission, better economic outcomes, and stronger democratic legitimacy," he said.
"Promising a specific interest rate path is what earned forward guidance a bad name," said the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis president.

"Rather than claim to know a single policy path in advance, a well-articulated framework should include a small number, perhaps two or three, of the most likely scenarios for inflation and employment, estimates of how probable each scenario is, and descriptions of how the policy rate would respond under each one," he said.
"As data and other information arrive, the scenarios and the likelihood of each are updated," he noted.

"Markets react to data through their expectations of how the central bank will respond to macroeconomic developments. The price of a Treasury bond reflects a forecast of the future policy path," he said.

"So when a central bank keeps its framework to itself, it does not free up markets to focus on data and other information. Rather, it forces market participants to guess how the central bank will assess the state of the economy and react to it."
"Guessing adds noise, which results in added premiums for uncertainty," noted Musalem. "Communicate the framework, and the opposite happens."

According to Musalem, the communications choice before them is not between noisy overpromising and stoic silence. It is a choice between leaving the public to guess how the central bank thinks and telling them.
"The most important thing a central bank can tell the public is not what it will do at the next few meetings. It is how and why it will decide as the economy unfolds," he concluded.
During the Q&A, Musalem said the Summary of Economic Projections, or the dot plot, is a tool to communicate the different policy paths, and it could be improved by connecting the dots.
"If we could connect the dots anonymously, I think that would provide the public with more information about different scenarios that the different policymakers are considering," he said.
